newsitem.title: USA: Organizations competing to rate the Web.
newsitem.headline: Organizations competing to rate the Web.

text.p: The drive to rate the content of Web sites is gaining momentum.

In the past year, three organisations have begun offering ratings services or label bureaus that identify Web sites based on age appropriateness or the amounts of sex, nudity, obscenity or violence they contain.
All three are based on the Platform for Internet Content Selection, or PICS, a protocol approved last year by the World Wide Web Consortium standards-setting body.

The newest of the bunch is NetShepherd (http://www.netshepherd.com/), a Calgary, Alberta, start-up that has reviewed and rated 300,000 Web sites to create a ratings database called a label bureau. Company officials hope to license it to online networks and publishers of Internet server and firewall software.

Two others, SafeSurf (http://www.safesurf.com/) in Van Nuys, Calif., and the non-profit group Recreational Software Advisory Council, or RSAC (http://www.rsac.org/) in Lexington, Mass., have rated more than 117,000 Web sites. The rivals are negotiating to include their respective self-rating services in Web browsers, Web search engines, Internet service providers, and national online networks.
It's only a matter of time before Internet surfers might log onto a Web directory and search all sites labeled "child," or "zero sex," or block out all un-rated Web sites.

"We're in deep discussions with InfoSeek, Lycos and Alta Vista right now," said Steve Balkam, executive director of the software advisory council. "These things can happen very quickly, or take months."

Ratings services differ from software programmes such as SurfWatch, Cyber Patrol and Net Nanny that block access to a pre-determined set of Web sites and Usenet newsgroups. Publishers of such "blacklist" software determine what sites are objectionable, often with input from users, and provide updated databases for a monthly fee.
Introduced in 1995, blacklist software provided one of the only means for users to block access to Web sites they deemed objectionable.

Its introduction was spurred in part by a public outcry over Internet pornography, which ultimately led to the passage of the Communications Decency Act in February 1996. The controversial law, vehemently opposed by Internet and civil-liberties groups, was subsequently overturned and is being appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court.

With the Web growing as quickly as it is, blacklist programmes aren't able to keep up, according to representatives of ratings services. Also, they said, programmes don't allow online communities, such as a universities, religious groups or customers of Internet service providers, to determine for themselves what they want or don't want to see.

As an alternative, RSAC introduced its RSACi Web rating system in April 1996. The rating system has four categories -- sex, nudity, language and violence. Each category has four levels, from "0" for none present, to "4" for most extreme. Publishers rate their own Web sites by completing an online form that directs them to describe the contents of their site.

But to date, only 17,000 of the hundreds of thousands of sites on the Web have used the RSACi rating system. Many of those are adult Web sites that see the benefit of having a selective audience, RSAC's Balkam said.
SafeSurf provides a similar self-rating service, though its rating system is more complex, with nine categories and nine levels within each category.

Close to 100,000 Web sites have used SafeSurf to rate themselves. SafeSurf Chairman Ray Soular is quick to admit the numbers could be much higher. He believes Web sites haven't bothered because Web directories aren't equipped to do searches based on ratings.
"If Alta Vista, Yahoo, Lycos and InfoSeek recognised (ratings) I believe the Web would be rated overnight," he said.

SafeSurf already has deals with CompuServe, Netcom On-Line Communications and another as-yet unnamed national Internet service provider to use its service, and is negotiating with Yahoo's Yahooligans kids' Web directory, Soular said.

Unlike SafeSurf and RSAC, NetShepherd chose to rate Web sites itself, hiring 400 Internet users to review and rate 750 sites each over an eight-week span. Web sites carry one of seven age-level labels -- general, child, pre-teen, teen, adult and objectionable.
"Then a parent or employer can decide what level of access they want to allow," said NetShepherd President Don Sandford.
Because it is based on the PICS protocol, NetShepherd's database -- and SafeSurf and RSACi ratings -- can be used with Microsoft's Internet Explorer Web browser, which also complies with PICS.
NetShepherd also is negotiating with online services and software publishers about licensing its database and expects to announce deals at the Internet World convention in March.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
